description: Prepared evergreen educational queue; factual claims require periodic rechecking; no claims of hands-on testing

articles.title: Where should you put a Wi-Fi router?
articles.dek: A room-by-room guide to improving wireless coverage before spending money on new hardware.
sections: Start with the actual problem

A router's position can make a noticeable difference to coverage, but it cannot fix every slow connection. Before moving equipment, check whether the problem affects every device or only a particular room. Test the same device near the router and again where performance is poor. If the speed and reliability improve nearby, wireless coverage is worth investigating.

Also check whether the internet provider has reported an outage. A device can be connected to Wi-Fi while its internet connection is unavailable. Fixing Wi-Fi placement will not repair a provider outage.
Choose a central, open location

For many homes, a reasonably central, elevated position gives the router more opportunity to reach rooms in different directions. Placing it behind a metal cabinet, inside a closet or close to large obstructions can interfere with the path between the router and devices.

You do not have to put the router in the geometric center of the house at any cost. Consider where people actually need connectivity, where the incoming connection is located, electrical safety and whether its antennas can be positioned according to the manufacturer's instructions.
Know what walls and floors change

Walls, floors and other building materials can attenuate wireless signals. The impact depends on the material, thickness, frequency band and layout. A signal that crosses multiple dense barriers may be less reliable than one with a clearer path. If you use equipment with multiple bands, experiment with the manufacturer-recommended settings before making broad changes.

A simple way to compare locations is to use the same device, stand in the same test spots and repeat comparable tasks after each change. Keep notes on room, position and whether the problem improved. That is more informative than relying on a single test result.
Compare three low-cost improvements

First, move the router out of an enclosure and away from large metal objects if practical. Second, position it where it is less obstructed by furniture and high-traffic household equipment. Third, if your home is larger or has difficult construction, consider wired access points or a properly configured mesh system only after confirming a coverage gap.
Avoid buying a new router simply because a speed-test score is disappointing. The limiting factor might be your internet plan, local device, an overcrowded channel or the destination service.
When placement is not enough

If the device is still slow near the router, investigate internet service, hardware condition and network configuration. If the router is far from a room and moving it is impractical, a wired Ethernet connection may be the most predictable option for fixed devices.

Never factory reset network equipment as a first troubleshooting step. Resetting can erase passwords, network settings and provider-specific configuration. Follow official instructions, and keep a record of symptoms before contacting support.
Quick decision checklist

Test two devices and two locations. Check for a provider outage. Move the router out of enclosed or obstructed locations. Repeat comparable tests. Only consider buying additional networking hardware if you have evidence of a coverage problem.

articles.title: kW vs. kWh: what your electricity bill actually measures
articles.dek: Understand power and energy, see the math, and estimate costs with a realistic example.
sources: U.S. Department of Energy — Estimating appliance energy use
sections: The short answer

A kilowatt (kW) describes a rate of power use. A kilowatt-hour (kWh) measures how much energy is used over time. Utility bills commonly include charges based on kilowatt-hours consumed. The distinction matters because two appliances with the same power rating can use very different amounts of energy depending on how long they run.
Convert watts into kilowatts

Power is often stated in watts. Divide a watt value by 1,000 to express the same power in kilowatts. A 100-watt load is 0.1 kW. A 1,500-watt load is 1.5 kW. The rating on an appliance may describe a maximum or nominal draw, not its continuous measured average.

If a device cycles on and off, such as a refrigerator or heater, simple nameplate estimates may overstate or understate actual consumption. A compatible energy meter or manufacturer-provided consumption data can make the estimate more useful.
Convert power and time into energy

Energy in kilowatt-hours is power in kilowatts multiplied by running time in hours. A hypothetical steady 100-watt device run for eight hours would use 0.8 kWh. Over 30 identical days, that would total 24 kWh.
A device run at twice the power for half the time can consume the same energy if all other factors are equal. That is why wattage alone cannot tell you what a device will cost over a month.
Estimate the part of the bill related to energy

Multiply estimated kWh by the relevant electricity rate in dollars per kWh. At an example rate of $0.15/kWh, 24 kWh would represent $3.60 in energy charges. Actual bills can also include fixed charges, seasonal rates, taxes, time-of-use pricing, demand charges or other utility-specific adjustments.

The site's calculator estimates energy cost, not your full utility bill. Use the exact rate and billing period from your utility when possible; avoid treating an arbitrary national average as your household price.
Why actual use can differ

Heating elements, compressors, electronic power supplies and other systems may change their electricity draw during operation. Standby modes can consume energy, and operating conditions matter. For a more accurate estimate, measure average consumption over a representative period instead of assuming the device draws its maximum wattage constantly.
Use the free tool

Open the electricity cost calculator on this site and try multiple wattage, hour and rate assumptions. Compare estimates before deciding whether a new device or a change in habits is financially worthwhile.

articles.title: Why is my phone charging slowly?
articles.dek: A practical checklist for checking cables, adapters, heat and charging settings safely.
sources: USB Implementers Forum — USB Power Delivery
sections: Separate normal slowdowns from faults

Many devices vary their charging speed throughout a charging session. Charging may slow as the battery approaches full, or when the device is warm. One measurement at an arbitrary battery percentage does not prove that a cable or adapter is defective.

If a device reports a charging or temperature warning, follow the device manufacturer's instructions before testing anything else. Stop using damaged, swollen, wet or unusually hot charging equipment.
Start with the power source

A computer USB port, a low-power adapter and a capable USB Power Delivery charger can offer very different charging capability. Check your phone's documented supported charging methods and compare them to the adapter specifications.
A higher number printed on a charger does not mean the phone will continuously draw that power. The phone, charger, cable and charging conditions all play a role.
Check the cable without guessing

USB-C describes connector shape, not a guarantee of particular current, transfer speed or charging protocol. Some cables are unsuitable for high-power or specialized uses. Read the printed rating or manufacturer specification rather than assuming all USB-C cables are identical.
Try a known-good manufacturer-compatible cable if one is available. Do not repair or continue using a cable with exposed conductors, melted insulation or damaged connectors.
Consider temperature, apps and settings

Charging can be affected by thermal management, wireless charging alignment and device settings. Heavy activities such as gaming or video recording may consume power while the device is charging and make the percentage rise more slowly.

If supported, check the device's battery health and optimized charging information. Device menus vary, so rely on the manufacturer manual for the exact setting names rather than following a generic sequence of taps.
When to seek service

Repeated unexpected shutdowns, excessive heat, physical battery damage or persistent charging errors warrant support from the device maker or an authorized service provider. Do not attempt to puncture or dismantle lithium-ion batteries.

For an ordinary slow-charge complaint, document the adapter, cable, battery level, temperature and approximate charge time before contacting support. Those details help avoid replacing perfectly good accessories.
Buying checklist

Before buying a new accessory, confirm the phone's supported input, charger output and the cable's verified rating. Compare a known-good setup first. Favor clear technical specifications and reliable return policies over unsupported speed claims.

articles.title: How large a power bank do you really need?
articles.dek: Understand watt-hours, capacity claims, losses and travel considerations before choosing portable charging.
sections: Start with your actual use case

A small battery pack that tops up a phone during commuting serves a different purpose from a large pack intended to keep multiple devices operating through a trip. Consider which devices you will charge, whether they need USB-C Power Delivery and how often you will have access to an outlet.
Do not choose solely by the biggest milliamp-hour number on the package. That single number does not describe output voltage, conversion losses or whether a device can negotiate the power it needs.
Understand mAh and Wh

Milliamp-hours (mAh) describe electric charge capacity at a stated voltage. Watt-hours (Wh) represent stored energy. To estimate watt-hours from a specified nominal voltage, multiply amp-hours by volts. Because devices use different nominal voltages, two mAh figures cannot always be compared directly.
For illustration, a 10,000 mAh pack rated at a nominal 3.7 volts corresponds to about 37 Wh of nominal stored energy (10 Ah × 3.7 V). This is not a claim about usable USB output energy.
Why you will not receive all the stated energy

Voltage conversion, heat, cable and connector losses, internal reserve, device charging circuitry and environmental conditions affect what reaches the connected device. For that reason, advertised capacity is not equivalent to the exact amount that can be delivered to your phone.

A useful comparison is the manufacturer's declared Wh rating alongside supported USB output ratings, physical size, quality and warranty. Real delivered capacity must be measured under specified conditions.
Check output capability separately

A battery pack's total capacity and maximum output power answer different questions. Capacity relates to how long it may supply energy; output rating relates to whether it can power or charge a particular device at the desired rate. Check the laptop or phone's requirements, the pack's port ratings and the cable's capability together.

Multiple devices plugged into one pack may share a total output budget. Look for manufacturer documentation that explains simultaneous charging limits rather than assuming every port reaches its advertised individual maximum.
Air travel and safety

Airline and aviation rules apply to lithium batteries and power banks, and restrictions depend on their watt-hour ratings and other conditions. Consult the FAA PackSafe rules and your airline before traveling. Do not rely on a generic social-media chart as your sole source.
Stop using a battery pack that is visibly swollen, leaking, damaged or abnormally hot. Keep it away from excessive heat and follow the manufacturer's handling instructions.
An efficient purchase decision

Write down device power needs, desired number of recharges, size/weight preference and travel restrictions. Compare verified Wh and output specs, then decide whether the extra capacity is worth carrying. More capacity is not always a better fit.

articles.title: 2.4 GHz vs. 5 GHz Wi-Fi: which should you use?
articles.dek: A practical guide to coverage, congestion, compatibility and choosing a Wi-Fi band.
sections: Different bands solve different needs

Many home networks support both 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz wireless bands. Broadly, 2.4 GHz often offers better range through obstacles in typical conditions, while 5 GHz can offer more channel capacity and higher throughput under suitable conditions. Actual results depend on the router, client, congestion, walls and local regulations.
A band name does not guarantee a speed. A poorly placed router on an uncongested band may outperform a newer one operating under heavy interference. Test your real devices where you use them.
When 2.4 GHz can be helpful

Some older or simpler connected devices support only 2.4 GHz. That band can also be practical where coverage matters more than peak data transfer. However, it is widely shared with other equipment and nearby wireless networks, so interference can still make performance poor.
If a smart-home accessory refuses to join the network, consult its manufacturer's setup instructions. Avoid disabling important security settings as a workaround.
When 5 GHz can be helpful

For devices relatively close to an access point and able to support it, 5 GHz often works well for high-throughput activities. The higher-frequency signal can weaken more over some walls and obstacles than a lower-frequency alternative.

It is not necessary to manually manage every device. Many routers use automatic band steering; manufacturer defaults may work well. Use simple comparisons rather than assuming the higher-numbered band always wins.
A fair comparison method

Use the same client and destination, test in the same room at roughly the same time, and repeat tests more than once. Look for repeatable differences in responsiveness and reliability, not just one peak result.
If problems occur only in a far room, think about router position or network coverage before assuming the band is incorrectly configured.
About Wi-Fi 6 and other names

Wi-Fi generation names describe sets of capabilities and are not interchangeable with frequency bands. Some newer equipment supports additional bands, but both the router and client must support the relevant features to benefit. Consult official manufacturer specifications for compatibility.
The practical answer

Leave band selection automatic when it works. If a specific device has a repeated problem, test the supported alternatives, verify security settings and document the outcome. Change one setting at a time so you can tell what made a difference.

articles.title: How much does an LED light bulb cost to run?
articles.dek: Use wattage and hours to compare lighting energy costs without confusing brightness and power.
sources: U.S. Department of Energy — Lighting choices to save money
U.S. Department of Energy — Estimating energy use
sections: Start with the actual wattage

Brightness and electricity use are not the same measure. The watt number describes the bulb's power use under specified conditions, while lumens describe the amount of visible light emitted. For comparing how much lighting costs to operate, the watt rating and hours of use matter most.
Read the specific lamp packaging or documentation instead of assuming all bulbs marketed as the same brightness consume the same number of watts.
A useful calculation

A hypothetical 9-watt lamp running five hours a day for 30 days consumes 1.35 kWh: 9 ÷ 1,000 × 5 × 30. At an example price of $0.15 per kWh, the energy portion of the monthly cost is about $0.20. Actual rates, run times and power use will differ.
A full household electricity bill often includes fixed fees and other charges; this example covers the bulb's estimated energy consumption alone.
Comparing two options fairly

If two light sources provide comparable useful illumination, comparing their electrical wattages is a reasonable starting point for energy costs. But wattage is not the only purchase consideration: brightness, beam direction, fit, color appearance, dimmer compatibility and expected lifespan matter too.
An inexpensive bulb that flickers with a particular dimmer or creates uncomfortable glare may be a poor purchase even if its running cost is low. Check compatibility and manufacturer recommendations.
How long the light is on matters

A light that runs for ten minutes a day has much less opportunity to affect energy costs than a light used for long evening hours. Estimate typical hours rather than multiplying every lamp by 24 hours.
For shared spaces or irregular schedules, take a representative week and note how often each light is used. That can make your assumptions more realistic.
Safety and compatibility

Use bulbs suited to the fixture's electrical and thermal ratings. Enclosed fixtures, outdoor locations and dimmers may have specific lamp requirements. Do not exceed the fixture's rated limits or modify electrical wiring without appropriate expertise.
Try the calculation yourself

Use the site's electricity cost calculator with your bulb's watts and your bill's rate. Then compare the estimated energy savings with the price of replacing a working bulb. This lets you decide based on your situation rather than an exaggerated savings claim.

articles.title: Wi-Fi connected but no internet? A practical troubleshooting guide
articles.dek: Find out whether the problem is your device, router, provider or public Wi-Fi sign-in before resetting settings.
sources: Microsoft Support — Fix Wi-Fi connection issues in Windows
Apple Support — If you can't connect to Wi-Fi on iPhone or iPad
Apple Support — Use captive Wi-Fi networks
sections: Why Wi-Fi can be connected while the internet is down

A Wi-Fi connection links your device to a nearby access point; it does not guarantee that the router or internet provider can reach websites. A device can therefore show strong signal bars while apps cannot load. First distinguish a complete outage from a single failed website or app. Try two unrelated sites and note the exact warning. If only one service fails while others work, investigate that service rather than immediately replacing equipment. A connection-status icon is useful evidence, but it is not a complete diagnosis.
Use two devices to locate the fault

Test a second phone or computer on the same Wi-Fi network. If both fail, investigate the router, modem and provider before changing either device. If only one fails, concentrate on that device. When possible, temporarily turn off Wi-Fi on a phone and test over cellular data, taking care not to use unexpected mobile data. If cellular works while every home Wi-Fi device fails, the websites are unlikely to be the shared cause. Record which devices and connections worked; this simple comparison often saves time and unnecessary purchases.
Check the provider and physical connection

Using cellular service if available, check your provider's official outage page or support channel. Look at the router and modem or fiber terminal for clearly labeled connection and alarm lights, interpreting them with the equipment manual. A working Wi-Fi light does not prove that the provider connection is healthy. Check accessible cables and power connections without opening equipment. Stop using damaged or unusually hot electrical accessories. If the provider reports an outage, wait for restoration rather than changing settings. Otherwise, follow the equipment maker's normal restart procedure and allow time to reconnect.
Restart safely; do not factory reset

A restart means switching equipment off and on as its manufacturer recommends. A factory reset is different: it can erase network names, passwords and customized provider settings. Do not press a recessed Reset button as a first troubleshooting step. If you have separate modem and router units, follow the provider's recommended restart order. Test the connection again before doing anything more complicated. If it returns, note what helped and stop changing settings. If it does not, keep the observations for a support call rather than repeating restarts indefinitely.
When only one device has the problem

Turn Wi-Fi off and on, reconnect to the correct network and restart the affected device. Check whether it works on another trusted Wi-Fi network. Windows users can run Microsoft's Network and Internet troubleshooter; iPhone and iPad users can inspect the Wi-Fi settings and any No Internet Connection message. Follow the linked official instructions because menus vary by operating-system version. Consider whether a recently enabled VPN, proxy, filtering app or security tool coincided with the problem. On managed work or school devices, ask the administrator before altering such settings or weakening protection.
Recognize DNS and IP-address clues

A device may reach its router but fail to translate website names into addresses, which can suggest a DNS problem. Microsoft documents checking network configuration, renewing an address and clearing the DNS resolver cache in Windows. An automatically assigned address beginning with 169.254 can indicate that the computer did not obtain the expected address through DHCP. Neither clue alone proves that the router is defective. Record existing settings before changing DNS or IP configuration. If your network uses fixed addresses, parental controls or business management, seek appropriate guidance rather than switching to arbitrary public DNS servers.
Public Wi-Fi may require a sign-in page

Hotels, airports and other public networks may let you join Wi-Fi but require a login or acceptance of terms before granting internet access. This is called a captive portal. Apple's guidance for iPhone and iPad is to select the network in Wi-Fi settings and wait for the login screen, or use Join Network when available. Use only the venue's legitimate portal; do not install unfamiliar certificates or profiles to make a hotspot work. Ask the venue for official instructions if the sign-in page never appears. This situation differs from a home broadband outage.
Escalate based on what the tests reveal

If several devices fail and the provider equipment shows an upstream problem, contact the provider with the outage time, indicator status and restart results. If one device fails on multiple otherwise-working networks, contact its manufacturer or IT support. Resetting network settings on an iPhone or iPad can remove saved Wi-Fi passwords and related cellular or VPN settings, so reserve it for later troubleshooting under Apple's instructions. If devices work near the router but not in a distant room, investigate wireless coverage instead. The goal is to isolate the failure before spending money, erasing settings or making disruptive changes.

articles.title: How much does a space heater cost to run? Calculate it before you plug in
articles.dek: Use your heater's wattage, actual running time and electricity rate to estimate daily and monthly costs, then check the safety rules that matter.
sources: U.S. Energy Information Administration — Measuring electricity
U.S. Energy Information Administration — Factors affecting electricity prices
U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission — Portable electric heater safety habits
U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission — Winter weather and portable heater safety
ENERGY STAR — Ductless heating and cooling
sections: The quick answer: watts, hours and your rate

A portable electric heater's running cost depends primarily on how much electrical power it draws, how long its heating element actually operates, and the price you pay per kilowatt-hour (kWh). A heater marked 1,500 watts draws about 1.5 kilowatts while operating at that rated input. At a purely illustrative electricity rate of $0.20 per kWh, one full-power hour costs about $0.30 in energy charges. Four full-power hours cost about $1.20. These are calculations, not measured results or a prediction of anyone's utility bill.

An adjustable thermostat complicates the estimate in a useful way: the heater may switch its heating element off after reaching the selected temperature. Four hours plugged in does not always mean four hours at full power. Start with the full-power estimate as a planning scenario, then refine it if you know the actual operating time.
Find the wattage before doing any math

Check the heater's rating label, manual or manufacturer specification for input power in watts (W). A unit may list different wattages for low and high settings; use the one you actually select. If the label lists electrical current and voltage instead, do not assume that multiplying those numbers gives an exact measured average power draw. The manufacturer's stated wattage is the safer starting point for a simple consumer estimate.

Do not confuse a heater's physical size, marketing name or advertised room coverage with electricity use. Two differently styled heaters can have the same rated wattage. Likewise, a timer setting tells you how long a unit is permitted to operate, not necessarily how long its heating element is energized.
Calculate cost with a three-step formula

First, divide watts by 1,000 to convert power to kilowatts. Second, multiply kilowatts by the hours the heater is drawing that power to obtain kilowatt-hours. Third, multiply kilowatt-hours by your electricity price in dollars per kWh. In one line: estimated energy cost = (watts ÷ 1,000) × full-power hours × electricity rate. The U.S. Energy Information Administration explains that watts measure power while kilowatt-hours measure electricity used over time.

For a monthly estimate, multiply the daily energy cost by the number of days used. Keep units visible as you calculate: 1,500 W ÷ 1,000 = 1.5 kW; 1.5 kW × 4 hours = 6 kWh; 6 kWh × $0.20/kWh = $1.20. Multiply $1.20 by 30 days to get $36 in hypothetical energy charges. The math assumes identical use every day, which rarely happens exactly.
Compare common settings without confusing them with measured use

At the same illustrative $0.20/kWh rate, a 750-watt setting running continuously for four hours uses 3 kWh and costs $0.60. A 1,000-watt setting over four full-power hours uses 4 kWh and costs $0.80. A 1,500-watt setting for four full-power hours uses 6 kWh and costs $1.20. Over 30 days of identical use, those scenarios correspond to $18, $24 and $36 in energy charges, respectively.

These examples do not mean the lower setting always costs less to maintain the same room temperature. A lower setting might run longer, while a higher setting might cycle off sooner. Room size, insulation, drafts, outdoor temperature, thermostat placement and the amount of heat already supplied by the home's heating system all influence the result.
What a thermostat changes—and what it does not

Suppose a 1,500-watt heater is switched on for four hours, but its heating element runs for only two of those hours because the thermostat cycles it on and off. Ignoring small additional consumption from controls or a fan, the heating element uses approximately 1.5 kW × 2 hours = 3 kWh, or $0.60 at the example rate. That is half the four-hour continuous-heating scenario.

Do not assume a 50 percent duty cycle just because a heater has a thermostat. During a cold spell, a heater in a drafty room may run almost continuously; in a well-insulated room it may cycle much less. If you cannot establish actual energized time, show a range of scenarios instead of presenting one precise monthly cost as fact. Never defeat safety controls to obtain a measurement.
Use the right electricity price from your bill

Look for your utility's price per kWh, then determine whether that number represents only an energy-supply charge or includes additional variable delivery charges. Some customers face time-of-use prices, seasonal rates, tiered usage charges or separate fixed fees. A fixed monthly customer charge usually will not change because you run one more appliance, but variable charges can. The EIA documents that electricity prices vary by location and customer type.

If your bill includes several variable per-kWh components, adding the applicable components may provide a better estimate of the extra cost than using only the advertised supply rate. If you have time-of-use pricing, estimate hours in each rate period separately and add them. Do not treat the example $0.20/kWh as a current national average or a price guaranteed for your home.
Ceramic, oil-filled and infrared: does the style change the bill?

Portable ceramic fan heaters, oil-filled radiators and many infrared room heaters commonly rely on electric resistance to create heat. At the same actual electrical energy use, there is no magic efficiency bonus that makes one resistance heater deliver dramatically more total heat into the room. Their differences often concern how quickly and where warmth is felt, whether a fan moves air, and how a thermostat manages operation.

An oil-filled heater does not burn its internal oil as fuel; the oil stores and distributes heat. An infrared heater can make a person or nearby surface feel warm without warming all the room air equally. Either may be more comfortable for a particular situation, but comfort is not a substitute for measured energy consumption. Compare wattage, safety features and appropriate use rather than relying on unsupported 'pennies a day' advertising.
Will a space heater save money compared with central heating?

Sometimes, but only under specific conditions. Heating one occupied room while safely reducing the heat delivered elsewhere might lower overall heating demand. Running a portable heater on top of an unchanged central heating schedule usually adds electricity consumption rather than replacing it. The outcome depends on your main heating fuel, equipment efficiency, home layout, heat loss, electricity tariff and whether other rooms can actually be kept cooler without causing problems.

Electric resistance heaters and heat pumps should not be treated as interchangeable. A heat pump moves heat instead of generating it solely through resistance, which can reduce electricity use for comparable heating needs under appropriate conditions. ENERGY STAR describes ductless heat pumps as an efficient option for suitable homes. For a single cold room, first check drafts, blocked vents and thermostat settings before assuming a second heater is the least expensive fix.
Safety is not optional when choosing a location or outlet

The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission advises keeping all sides of a portable heater at least three feet from bedding, curtains, furniture, papers and other combustible items. Put it on a stable, level surface where children or pets will not knock it over. Keep it away from water. Plug an electric portable heater directly into a suitable wall outlet—not a power strip or extension cord—and do not route its cord beneath a rug or carpet.

Never leave a portable heater running while you sleep or when it is unattended. If its plug or cord becomes hot, disconnect it and seek qualified service; if the wall outlet itself is hot, contact a qualified electrician. Do not use a heater with a damaged cord, plug or housing. Before using an older or secondhand model, check official recall information. A bargain electricity estimate is never a reason to ignore these precautions.
A five-minute decision checklist

Write down the heater's rated watts and the setting you plan to use. Choose a realistic number of full-power hours per day, not just the number of hours it is plugged in. Find the relevant variable price per kWh on your bill. Calculate daily and monthly energy cost for a high-use and a lower-use scenario. Finally, check whether the heater can be positioned and connected safely without extension cords, power strips or combustible materials nearby.

Use Practical Pick's free electricity cost calculator to compare wattage, hours and your own rate; the result is an energy-only estimate, not a forecast of your entire utility bill. If the predicted cost is too high, consider addressing drafts or evaluating your existing heating system rather than shopping for a supposedly miraculous resistance heater. The best decision combines realistic energy math, comfort and safe operation.

articles.title: Wi-Fi extender vs. mesh vs. access point: which fixes a dead zone?
articles.dek: Compare a range extender, mesh Wi-Fi and a wired access point using your home's layout, backhaul quality and a simple before-and-after test.
sources: Google Home and Nest Help — Where to place your Wi-Fi devices
Google Home and Nest Help — Mesh test and performance
TP-Link Support — Is your range extender working and in the right spot?
ASUS Support — Ethernet backhaul between AiMesh routers
FTC Consumer Advice — How to secure your home Wi-Fi network
sections: Which option actually fixes a Wi-Fi dead zone?

A range extender may be enough for one room just beyond good router coverage. A coordinated mesh system can be more convenient when several rooms or floors need stronger coverage. A wired access point is often the best technical fit when Ethernet already reaches the problem area, especially when thick walls make wireless links unreliable. None of these devices can repair an internet service outage or guarantee a particular speed.

The key difference is backhaul: the connection from your new Wi-Fi device back to the main network. A wireless extender or mesh point needs a good wireless link to the router. A wired access point uses Ethernet for that connection. Choosing based on the backhaul, not the largest advertised speed number, prevents many disappointing purchases.
Confirm that the problem is coverage, not the internet service

Use the same laptop or phone in three places: close to the router, partway toward the troublesome room, and inside that room. Repeat the same website visit, video call or speed test at roughly similar times. Write down dropped connections, long loading delays and inconsistent results. Repeat with another device. If only one device has trouble in a location where others work, troubleshoot that device first.

If performance is poor even beside the router, an extender will not address the likely cause. Check for a provider outage, router issues and wired performance if a wired device is available. If connections are consistently good near the router and poor at the far end of the home, coverage and obstacles are reasonable suspects. Change one thing at a time so you can identify what helped.
Why backhaul matters more than Wi-Fi bars

Your phone may show a strong connection to a nearby extender even while the extender has a weak connection to the main router. The phone-to-extender link is only one part of the journey. Wireless backhaul shares radio resources and can be affected by interference, distance, walls and the hardware's radio design. This is why moving a node closer to the router sometimes improves service in the far room even though the node itself is farther away.

Ethernet backhaul avoids the wireless hop between the main router and an additional access point. ASUS documents Ethernet backhaul as an option to improve bandwidth and stability between compatible AiMesh devices. That does not mean every mesh kit supports it or that every wired connection will be fast; verify ports, cable condition and the exact manufacturer's configuration instructions.
When a range extender makes sense

A range extender connects to an existing wireless network and expands its reach. It can be a reasonable low-complexity choice when one room needs modest connectivity and an outlet is available in a location that still receives a healthy router signal. Some extenders also support Ethernet or access-point mode, but features vary. Check the specifications of the exact model rather than assuming the label 'extender' tells you everything.

Placement matters. TP-Link recommends starting roughly halfway between the router and the weak area, still inside the router's useful coverage. Placing an extender in the dead zone itself can leave it with an unreliable upstream link. Check its signal or connection-status indicator and test real activities from the destination room. If the extender broadcasts a different network name, verify that your device has actually connected to it.
When a mesh system makes sense

Mesh systems coordinate a main router and compatible additional nodes. They can simplify coverage across several rooms or floors, but the term 'mesh' does not promise seamless roaming or compatibility across brands and generations. Google notes, for example, that Nest Wifi Pro cannot be combined in one mesh with older Nest Wifi or Google Wifi devices. Verify the exact product family's compatibility before buying add-on nodes.

Start with the minimum number of nodes that might solve the problem. Google's placement guidance says nodes need a strong connection to each other and should generally sit partway toward weak areas, not at the farthest edge. If the system offers a mesh-link test, run it after placement changes. More nodes are not automatically better: a weak upstream link can remain the bottleneck regardless of how many signal bars a device displays.
When a wired access point is the stronger choice

A wired access point uses Ethernet to connect back to the existing network and broadcasts Wi-Fi near the devices that need it. If you already have Ethernet in a home office, upstairs room or basement, this is worth considering before a wireless repeater. Some compatible mesh nodes can use Ethernet backhaul as well, giving you coordinated management with a wired link.

Follow the manufacturer's access-point or bridge-mode instructions. For an ordinary home setup, you generally want the existing main router to continue handling routing and local address assignment, rather than accidentally creating a second independent router and DHCP service. If running new cable inside walls or between buildings is required, use an appropriate qualified installer and wiring rather than treating an indoor patch cable as a permanent building installation.
Match the solution to your home's layout

One bedroom with weak Wi-Fi but a good signal in the hallway: first try moving the router, then consider a well-placed extender. Several distant rooms across two floors: a compatible mesh system may make coverage easier to manage, provided nodes can maintain strong links. A detached workspace or a room behind dense masonry with an existing wired route: a wired access point may be more dependable than attempting to repeat a weak signal.

These are decision examples, not measured performance rankings. If the whole house is slow, investigate the service and router before adding nodes. If only a printer or television fails while other devices work beside it, check that device's Wi-Fi capabilities and settings. In a rental where cabling is not possible, wireless placement may be the practical compromise even if wired backhaul would otherwise be preferable.
Place the new device for a good upstream connection

Try a central, open, elevated location for the main router where practical. Keep it away from large metal obstructions and avoid enclosing it in furniture. For an extender or wireless mesh point, start between the router and the weak room, then adjust the location gradually. Both Google's mesh guidance and TP-Link's extender guidance emphasize maintaining a strong connection back to the router.

If moving a node one room closer to the router improves performance in the far room, the original placement may have weakened its backhaul. If a thick wall blocks every possible wireless path, a different access-point location or wired route may be necessary. Coverage estimates on retail packaging are not guarantees for a particular floor plan, building material or neighboring wireless environment.
How to verify that your fix really worked

Repeat the same three-location test you performed before installation. Use the same device, repeat tests and compare typical performance rather than one peak result. Check whether video calls remain stable, whether pages load consistently and whether the device reconnects reliably after moving through the house. If your network app reports which node a device uses, verify that the client is actually connected to the expected one.

Inspect the extender's status or the mesh system's link-quality report as well. Google's mesh test guidance explains that a weak connection between points can limit performance for devices connected through that point. Strong Wi-Fi bars at the far end do not prove that the upstream connection is healthy. If results remain poor, move the node, check its backhaul or revisit the original diagnosis before buying more equipment.
Do not trade away network security for coverage

Keep router firmware current and use WPA3 Personal when supported, or WPA2 Personal where needed. The Federal Trade Commission recommends those security modes, strong administrative credentials and updated router software. Do not disable encryption or switch to obsolete WEP or WPA security simply to make an old accessory connect. Check the security and band requirements of older smart-home devices before changing settings for the entire household.

Confirm compatibility with your existing router, the exact mesh family, Ethernet backhaul support and any access-point mode you need. Do not assume every device marketed as 'mesh compatible' works with every other product. Check the current manufacturer's compatibility documentation and update policies. Keep a record of your original network settings so you can reverse an unsuccessful configuration change without resorting immediately to a factory reset.
Buying checklist and bottom line

Before spending money, record the router model, the rooms that fail, the results near and far from the router, whether Ethernet outlets exist, and where a wireless node could receive a good signal. Decide whether the goal is one extra room or multiple floors. Compare actual backhaul options, security support, compatibility, installation requirements and return policies. Avoid choosing solely by maximum advertised wireless speed.

A range extender is a practical possibility for a small gap with good nearby signal. Mesh can suit multiple rooms when nodes can be placed well. A wired access point is especially attractive where a cable already exists or wireless obstacles are severe. If moving the router solves the problem, buy nothing. Whatever you choose, the best result is reliable service where you use it, demonstrated by a repeatable before-and-after test.

articles.title: Why Does My Phone Stop Charging at 80%? Check the Setting Before Replacing Anything
articles.dek: An 80% charging pause may be intentional. Check iPhone, Pixel and Galaxy battery limits, heat warnings and real charging faults in the right order.
sources: Apple Support — Charge Limit and Optimized Battery Charging
Apple Support — If your iPhone won't charge
Apple Support — iPhone and iPad temperature behavior
Google Pixel Help — Get the most life from your Pixel battery
Samsung Support — Galaxy Battery protection in One UI 6.1
sections: The short answer: 80% is often a feature, not a fault

If your phone repeatedly pauses at about 80% while otherwise charging normally, first check its battery-protection settings. Many modern phones intentionally limit how long their batteries remain fully charged. A fixed limit and a delayed finish are different: a fixed limit can hold the charge near 80% until you change it, while an adaptive feature may wait and finish charging before you normally unplug.

Heat is another reason charging can slow or pause near that level. A phone that pauses only in a warm car or while running navigation needs a different investigation from one that stops at precisely the same percentage every night. The number alone cannot prove a cable, charger or battery has failed. Start with the screen message and model-specific settings, not a purchase.
First, distinguish a limit, a delay and a fault

Situation one: the battery reaches roughly 80% consistently, a battery-health setting is enabled, and no warning appears. That points toward an intentional charge limit. Situation two: the phone says charging is optimized, shows an estimated completion time, or resumes later. That points toward a scheduled or adaptive delay. Situation three: charging pauses unpredictably, the device is unusually warm, or a temperature or accessory warning appears. Treat that as a potential environmental or hardware issue.

Write down the phone model, software version, percentage where charging stops, whether you use wired or wireless charging, any message, and whether charging resumes after cooling. These observations are more informative than repeatedly disconnecting and reconnecting the cable. Avoid a factory reset, battery replacement or new high-wattage charger before distinguishing these cases.
iPhone 15 and later: inspect Charge Limit

Apple provides a configurable Charge Limit on iPhone 15 models and later. Open Settings, select Battery, then Charging. You can choose a limit from 80% to 100% in 5% steps. When a limit below 100% is selected, the phone normally stops within a few percentage points of that limit. Apple also says it may occasionally charge to 100% to maintain accurate battery estimates. An occasional full charge therefore does not necessarily mean the limit has failed.

If you need extra capacity for travel, change the limit using the supported charging screen rather than assuming the adapter is defective. On supported software, a temporary override may also be available. Menu labels can change with software releases, so consult Apple's current instructions for your model. If the limit is already 100%, check optimized charging, temperature and accessories instead.
Older iPhones: understand Optimized Battery Charging

On iPhone 14 and earlier, Apple documents Optimized Battery Charging under Settings, Battery, then Battery Health & Charging. The feature learns charging routines and may delay charging beyond 80% when it predicts the phone will stay plugged in for a long time. It is not a permanent 80% cap. When active, a notification can indicate when the phone expects to finish, and Apple documents a Charge Now option for completing charging sooner.

Prediction-based charging may behave differently on a weekend trip, during shift work or after a routine change. On newer iPhones, Apple makes Optimized Battery Charging available when Charge Limit is set to 100%. Disabling optimization solely to make the percentage rise sooner may increase battery wear over time. Choose based on when you actually need a full charge.
Google Pixel: compare Limit to 80% and Adaptive Charging

Google documents Charging optimization under Settings, Battery, Battery health, then Charging optimization on supported Pixel phones. Pixel 6a and later devices can offer Limit to 80%, which prioritizes long-term battery health. Adaptive Charging is different: it aims to finish a 100% charge near when you are likely to unplug. Google says Adaptive Charging may need about 14 days to learn your habits and may not activate when your routine changes.

Google also describes automatic battery protection during prolonged charging or high-temperature conditions on certain Pixels, which may limit charging to around 70–80% and show a protection message. If a Pixel occasionally reaches 100% even with an 80% limit, Google says periodic full charges help keep capacity estimates accurate. Use the current Pixel support page for your exact model instead of following screenshots from a different Android version.
Samsung Galaxy: check Battery protection mode

Samsung's One UI 6.1 documentation describes Basic, Adaptive and Maximum Battery protection modes. On supported models, Maximum stops charging at 80%; Adaptive uses protective behavior during expected sleep and changes behavior before waking; Basic allows a full charge and resumes charging after the level falls. Samsung lists the path as Settings, Battery, Battery protection, but cautions that available features vary by model.

Some Galaxy phones running older software used an 85% protection limit instead. That distinction matters when an online tip claims every Galaxy should stop at 80%. Confirm the actual software and mode selected. If Maximum is enabled and you need a full charge for a particular day, choose a supported alternative mode. A new charging cable will not override a software-imposed limit.
Heat and cold can temporarily pause charging

Apple says charging can slow or stop when an iPhone becomes too hot or too cold, including during wireless charging. Common heat-producing situations include navigation, games, direct sunlight and other demanding activity while charging. Apple documents a typical operating ambient range of 32–95°F (0–35°C) for iPhone and iPad, although internal temperature and other conditions also matter. A parked car can become too hot even when the outdoor air feels comfortable.

If the screen shows Charging On Hold or a temperature warning, follow that warning. Move the phone away from direct sunlight, stop demanding apps, and allow it to return gradually to normal temperature. Never refrigerate, freeze or rapidly chill a hot phone. A swollen battery, leaking fluid, smoke, or physically damaged charging equipment is not a settings issue: stop using it and seek qualified manufacturer or service guidance.
When the percentage is unpredictable, check the charging path

A software limit is less likely when charging cuts in and out at random percentages, the cable must be held at an angle, or the phone reports an unsupported accessory. Inspect the adapter, cable and connector for visible damage. Apple recommends checking for secure connections, using a wall outlet and trying another compatible cable or charger when appropriate. Do not continue using equipment with exposed conductors, bent prongs, melting or unusual heat.

If the port appears obstructed, follow the device maker's cleaning instructions rather than inserting metal tools or liquid into it. With wireless charging, confirm that the phone is aligned on a compatible charger and remove interfering accessories according to manufacturer guidance. Restarting and checking for applicable software updates can be reasonable after basic checks; a full factory reset should not be the first diagnostic step.
A controlled test that avoids unnecessary purchases

First, note the existing charge limit or adaptive setting and any warning. Second, use a known-good compatible charger in a cool indoor room without gaming or navigation. Third, observe whether charging reaches the selected limit, pauses with a clear message or stops unpredictably. Fourth, if you intentionally need 100%, use the manufacturer's supported temporary override or change the limit, then observe whether the phone passes the previous stopping point.

Change only one factor at a time. Swapping the cable, adapter, wireless pad and software settings simultaneously makes the cause difficult to identify. You do not need to drain a phone to zero or leave it plugged in overnight just to run this test. If charging behaves normally after changing a documented limit, you have a useful explanation without buying replacement hardware.
Should you leave the 80% limit on?

An 80% limit trades some usable charge on a given day for less time spent at a high state of charge. It may suit someone who ends most days with substantial battery remaining or keeps the phone connected to power for long periods. If your schedule includes travel, long shifts, frequent navigation or unreliable access to outlets, the extra capacity of a full charge may matter more on those days.

There is no universal rule requiring every phone to remain between two exact percentages at all times. Follow the options for your model, avoid excessive heat, and choose a charging routine that supports your actual use. The purpose is to reduce unnecessary battery stress without making the phone less useful.
When to contact support, and a quick decision checklist

Contact the manufacturer or an authorized repair provider if charging still fails with a compatible known-good setup, warnings persist in normal conditions, the port appears damaged, or the battery is swollen or otherwise physically abnormal. Give support the model, software version, exact warning, stopping percentage, charging method and tests already performed. This can prevent an unnecessary replacement that does not address the problem.

Stops near 80% every time? Check the configured limit. Pauses overnight but reaches 100% later? Check adaptive charging. Stops while warm or shows Charging On Hold? Let it return to normal temperature and follow the warning. Stops at random levels or reports an accessory error? Check the cable, adapter and connection. Still failing? Seek manufacturer guidance. This is an explanation of documented features, not a claim of hands-on testing.

articles.title: How Much Electricity Does a Dehumidifier Use? Calculate the Real Cost
articles.dek: Estimate dehumidifier running costs from watts, hours and your electric rate, then use capacity and efficiency ratings to choose wisely.
sources: ENERGY STAR — Dehumidifier testing and capacity
U.S. Department of Energy — Estimating appliance and home electronic energy use
sections: The short answer: watts, hours and electricity rate

A dehumidifier uses electricity to move air and, for a typical refrigerant-based portable unit, operate a refrigeration system that condenses moisture. Its energy cost depends on the power it draws, how long it actually runs and your utility's price per kilowatt-hour (kWh). There is no single reliable monthly dollar amount for every dehumidifier: room moisture, temperature, settings and equipment efficiency all matter.

Use this formula for a first estimate: watts ÷ 1,000 × operating hours × dollars per kWh. If you know the appliance's rated watts but not its actual average draw, treat the answer as a scenario rather than a measured bill. A humidistat may stop and restart the compressor, so hours plugged in are not necessarily hours at full power.
Worked example: a 400-watt unit

Suppose a hypothetical dehumidifier draws 400 watts while actively operating. If it draws that power for eight hours in one day, its energy use is 0.4 kW × 8 hours = 3.2 kWh. At an illustrative electricity rate of $0.18 per kWh, the energy charge is $0.576, or about $0.58 for that day. Repeat the same use for 30 days and the calculation gives 96 kWh and $17.28 in energy charges.

Now compare a much heavier-use scenario: the same 400-watt draw for 16 hours per day over 30 days equals 192 kWh and $34.56 at that same illustrative rate. Neither example is a forecast for your home, and neither includes fixed utility fees or rate tiers. The important lesson is that operating time can change the answer as much as the equipment's wattage.
Find your own electricity rate before estimating

Look for the per-kWh energy charge on your utility bill, including any applicable variable delivery charges if you want to estimate the marginal cost of extra electricity use. Some bills have time-of-use periods, seasonal pricing, tiered rates or credits, so a single rate can be an approximation. Avoid substituting a national average when your actual bill is available.

If your bill shows total dollars divided by total kWh, that blended figure may include fixed fees that would not increase when the dehumidifier runs. For an incremental-cost estimate, use the charges that actually vary with consumption. If pricing changes by hour, calculate each time block separately and add the results.
Measure use instead of assuming nonstop operation

A plug-in energy meter rated for the appliance's electrical load can record accumulated kWh over several days. Follow the meter and dehumidifier instructions, use a suitable grounded outlet and never exceed the meter's rating. A week that includes damp and dry days is more informative than a short measurement during a single compressor cycle.

Record the meter's starting and ending kWh readings and the dates. Divide the difference by the number of days to find average daily energy use; multiply by your relevant rate for an estimated daily cost. Repeat during a wetter period if you want a more representative seasonal range. Do not treat the compressor's nameplate wattage as a measured daily average.
Why humidity, temperature and settings change consumption

A damp basement, laundry area or room with an ongoing moisture source may require more moisture removal than a relatively dry room. A humidistat can reduce runtime once its target is reached, while a lower target may keep the equipment working longer. Actual behavior depends on the model and conditions; track indoor relative humidity rather than adjusting settings blindly.

Temperature also matters. ENERGY STAR notes that conventional refrigerant dehumidifiers can experience coil frosting when the surrounding air is below about 65°F, and that lower-temperature-capable or automatic defrost models may be appropriate. If a unit repeatedly frosts, follow its instructions instead of assuming continuous operation is effective moisture removal.
Capacity in pints per day is not the same as electricity use

Dehumidifier capacity, often listed as pints per day, describes water removal under specified test conditions. It is not a power rating and cannot be converted directly into a monthly electricity bill. A higher-capacity unit may remove more water in a shorter time, but the right choice depends on how damp and large the space is.

Be careful when comparing an older machine's advertised capacity with a new model. ENERGY STAR explains that test-condition changes beginning around 2020 led to lower-looking capacity ratings on some otherwise comparable portable units. Compare units using current, consistent test methods and the manufacturer's specifications, not just the biggest printed pint number.
Read the efficiency rating: liters per kWh

ENERGY STAR explains dehumidifier efficiency using integrated energy factor (IEF), expressed in liters of water removed per kilowatt-hour. Higher IEF generally means more moisture removed per unit of energy under standardized test conditions. That makes it more useful for comparing efficiency than comparing wattage alone, especially when capacities differ.

ENERGY STAR's current dehumidifier criteria took effect October 1, 2025. Its product listings and criteria can help you compare certified models by capacity and efficiency. A certification or lab rating is not a promise that every household will achieve the same runtime or savings; actual room conditions and use patterns still matter.
Lower operating cost by addressing the moisture source

Before purchasing a larger machine, look for obvious sources of unwanted water: plumbing leaks, seepage, blocked drainage or wet materials. A dehumidifier can remove moisture from air, but it is not a substitute for fixing a leak or persistent water intrusion. Investigate unexplained dampness and use qualified help for structural, electrical or significant water-damage problems.

Keep the unit's intake and exhaust clear according to its manual, clean filters as directed and maintain its bucket or drain system. Place it on an appropriate stable surface with the manufacturer's required clearance. A clogged filter or poorly arranged drain can undermine performance even if the device is still consuming electricity.
When buying a replacement makes sense

If you already own a functioning dehumidifier, estimate its measured annual kWh before deciding that a more efficient model will pay for itself. For example, an illustrative 100-kWh annual reduction at $0.18/kWh saves $18 in variable energy charges per year. Compare that with the purchase cost, expected service life, capacity, drainage features, noise and warranty; do not claim a guaranteed payback from an efficiency label alone.

For a new purchase, first identify the room's approximate size and moisture conditions, then use ENERGY STAR's sizing guidance and certified-product information. Confirm the model is suitable for the operating temperature and has a convenient bucket or continuous-drain option. Buy for the moisture problem you actually have rather than choosing the largest unit by default.
Quick checklist before you decide

Check your bill for a useful per-kWh rate. Find the dehumidifier's wattage or measure kWh with a properly rated meter. Record realistic active operating hours and calculate a range rather than one exact monthly figure. Check whether the room has a leak or drainage problem, and monitor humidity and frost behavior.

If replacing equipment, compare current capacity ratings and integrated energy factor, not just marketing claims. Use Practical Pick's electricity-cost calculator to try multiple wattages, runtimes and rates. A calculation informed by your own measurements is more valuable than a generic promise of savings.

articles.title: How Much Electricity Does a Ceiling Fan Use? Calculate the Cost
articles.dek: Calculate ceiling fan electricity costs using watts, hours and your rate, and learn when fans can help lower air-conditioning bills.
sources: U.S. Department of Energy — Estimating appliance energy use
ENERGY STAR — Installation and usage tips
sections: Calculate the cost using watts and hours

A ceiling fan consumes electricity to run its motor; a built-in light may add a separate load. There is no universal fan wattage because motor design, blade size, speed and lighting differ. Find your model's published wattage at the setting you actually use. Divide watts by 1,000, multiply by hours of operation, then multiply by your electricity rate per kilowatt-hour (kWh). This estimates variable energy charges rather than the entire utility bill. The U.S. Department of Energy describes the same method for estimating household appliance energy use.

A fan rated at 50 watts, used eight hours daily for 30 days, consumes 12 kWh. At an illustrative $0.20 per kWh, that costs $2.40 for the month. These are hypothetical inputs, not a national electricity price or a claim about typical fan power. If that same fan operates continuously for 30 days, its 36 kWh would cost $7.20 at the example rate. Actual power and rates can differ substantially.
Low, medium and high speed are not equivalent

A ceiling fan generally draws different amounts of power at different speeds, so a high-speed rating may overstate your normal consumption if you use low speed. Check manufacturer specifications or a certified product listing for speed-specific watts. ENERGY STAR model listings can identify low-speed, high-speed and standby power. The relevant figure is the motor's draw under the conditions you use, not the largest number on a box.

For mixed use, calculate each setting separately. Suppose a hypothetical fan uses 15 watts on low for six hours and 50 watts on high for two hours. Its daily use is (15 × 6 + 50 × 2) ÷ 1,000, or 0.19 kWh. Multiply by your rate for the energy cost. This approach is more defensible than assuming eight hours at maximum speed, but still depends on reliable wattage inputs.
Include the light kit without double counting

Some fans have integrated lights, while others have separate bulbs. A fan-motor specification may exclude lighting electricity, so read the label carefully. If the motor draws 40 watts and the lamps together draw 18 watts, both operating simultaneously would use about 58 watts under those assumed conditions. If the light is off, do not include its 18 watts. If a published total already includes lighting, do not add it again.

Changing to a compatible lower-wattage lamp may reduce the lighting portion of electricity use without changing motor consumption. Compare bulb wattage and lumens, and check fixture ratings, dimmer compatibility and enclosed-fixture restrictions. Do not exceed the fixture's specified electrical or thermal limits.
Can a fan reduce air-conditioning costs?

A ceiling fan circulates air and can make people feel cooler through airflow. It does not remove heat from the room as an air conditioner does. ENERGY STAR advises turning fans off in unoccupied rooms because fans cool people, not rooms. Running an empty-room fan typically adds electricity use without delivering a comfort benefit to anyone.

The larger potential savings come when airflow allows you to raise the air-conditioner thermostat while remaining comfortable. Whether that saves money depends on the thermostat adjustment, climate, occupancy and cooling-system efficiency. If the thermostat stays unchanged, running the fan usually adds to total electricity use. Avoid promising a fixed dollar saving without measuring the household's actual conditions.
Compare efficiency using airflow per watt

ENERGY STAR evaluates ceiling-fan efficiency using airflow per watt, expressed as cubic feet per minute per watt (CFM/W), under defined test conditions. This is more informative than watts alone because a very low-power fan may also move little air. Compare similar fan types and their airflow, room fit, sound and controls rather than simply selecting the smallest watt number.

A certified product listing may provide low-speed and high-speed power values and other performance measurements. ENERGY STAR also publishes criteria for standard ceiling fans and low-profile hugger fans. The most efficient choice for a particular room is not necessarily the cheapest or the one with the longest blades. Room dimensions, mounting height and user comfort matter.
Find your real usage without unsafe electrical work

Identify the exact model number, consult its manufacturer manual or ENERGY STAR listing, and record realistic daily hours for each speed. Read your utility bill for the applicable energy rate. If your plan has time-of-use prices, calculate separately for expensive and inexpensive periods. Keep the light's operating hours separate from the motor's if they differ.

Most ceiling fans are hardwired. Do not remove wiring or improvise a plug connection merely to use a household plug-in energy meter. If precise measurement of a hardwired fan is important, consult a qualified electrician. Otherwise, describe the result as an estimate based on manufacturer data, not a measured electricity bill reduction.
Install and operate safely through the seasons

ENERGY STAR advises using a ceiling-fan-rated electrical box and following the manufacturer's mounting and clearance instructions. A box intended only for a light fixture may not support a fan's weight and movement. If wiring, mounting support or ceiling clearance is uncertain, use a qualified installer rather than attempting an improvised repair.

For summer use, ENERGY STAR recommends counterclockwise rotation that creates a downward breeze when viewed from below. In winter, low-speed clockwise rotation can produce a gentle updraft and circulate warm air near the ceiling. Confirm the actual airflow and consult your specific fan's manual, because controls differ. Turn the fan off when the room is empty.
Decide whether replacement is worthwhile

Calculate annual energy use using your real schedule before spending money on a replacement. For example, a hypothetical 50-watt fan running eight hours every day for 365 days consumes 146 kWh. At the illustrative $0.20 rate, that is $29.20 annually in energy charges. A more efficient model could reduce that amount, but savings depend on the difference in measured wattage and actual use.

If the existing fan is reliable and comfortable, electricity savings alone may not quickly recover the cost of buying and installing another one. Noise, airflow, lighting, controls and safety can be better reasons to replace it. Use the Practical Pick electricity-cost calculator to compare scenarios, and avoid treating a manufacturer efficiency label as proof of your personal savings.
